newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: PHILIPPINES CUTS OVERNIGHT RATES, RAISES RESERVES.
newsitem.headline: PHILIPPINES CUTS OVERNIGHT RATES, RAISES RESERVES.

text.p: The Philippine central bank said on Wednesday it is cutting its closely-watched overnight borrowing rate to 14.0 percent from 18.0 percent effective Thursday.
It will also reduce its overnight lending rate to 18.0 percent from 22.0 percent.

"Since we are more than convinced that we have gained headway in tempering speculative play in the foreign exchange market, it is timely that central bank rates be further reduced," central bank governor Gabriel Singson said in a statement.
The central bank also raised banks' liquidity reserves on deposits and trust funds to five percent from four percent.
The move is expected to contract domestic liquidity by about 10.6 billion, Singson said.

The central bank's five-day, two-week and one-month reverse repo rates were also being cut to 12.0 percent from 13.0 percent, while the two-month reverse repo rate was being trimmed to 12.25 percent from 13.5 percent.
The three-month reverse repo rate will be reduced to 12.5 percent from 13.75 percent.
"This new set of monetary measures is expected to support the central bank's delicate balancing of growth and inflation objectives," Singson said.
"Monetary policy recognises the flexibility afforded by low inflation to accommodate growth," he added.
Traders said the central bank had been implementing this twin strategy of cutting rates and raising reserves as an inexpensive way of curtailing peso speculation.

Since late July, the central bank had doubled liquidity reserves to four percent. The liquidity reserves are the portion of the reserve requirement that should be placed in short-term, market-yielding securities issued by the central bank.

The central bank last month raised its overnight borrowing rate to a 2 1/2-year high of 32 percent in a futile defence of the peso which fell prey to the currency turmoil in the region. The peso had a de facto devaluation on July 11.
The high domestic interest rates had raised concerns among companies that these could cripple business activity and lead to a recession.

On Wednesday, the peso succumbed to fresh selling following a renewed attack on other regional currencies. The central bank said it had sold only $4 million to curb the peso depreciation which went as low as 29.10 early in the session.
The domestic stock market has been wallowing in negative territory in recent days due to uncertainties in the currency market.
